content:
Hey all!

My name is Safal, and I'm a recent graduate in mathematics and philosophy. I was originally intending to go to graduate school to study logic and the philosophy of mathematics, but life got in the way. Alas, I never lost my interest in proofs and formalization! When OpenAI dropped its collection of hundreds of (putatively) Lean-verified proofs (and weeks before claimed to have solved Navier-Stokes), there was a lot of spectacle; but the mathematical community at large lamented having little to no understanding of the architecture of these proofs.

To mitigate this, I decided to treat this massive pile of compiled Lean proofs as empirical data to see what patterns we could uncover. I wrote up the methodology and my initial findings in a preprint here: [https://github.com/safsom/math-ai-projects/blob/main/report/report.pdf].

To compare proofs across completely different areas of math, I threw out all names and specific definitions, keeping only the bare logical skeleton of each inference step. That let me measure which combinations of steps the AI leans on compared to human authors. I also looked closely at how proofs use intermediate claims (have statements). I adopt the (admittedly normative) principle that a lemma is only supposed to exist if it makes the proof clearer or shorter by being reused. Because substituting every lemma directly into a proof can cause it to explode in size, I measured the exact size of each proof in four states: as written, with every lemma expanded out, in an optimal layout that keeps only the lemmas that actually save space, and with every repeated subproof reused as much as possible.

As far as the actual data goes, I compiled 96 randomly selected projects from openai/math (around 36,000 theorems), three smaller AI corpora (Gauss's sphere packing, AxiomProver's Putnam solutions, and Aristotle's IMO solutions), and two human research projects (Carleson and sphere eversion) against mathlib commit d13f23b (this was as much as my MacBook Air with 8GB of RAM could handle). The data shows that AI proofs are (maybe not) surprisingly bad at reusing their own work (what I call "compressing" their proofs). In particular, under the metrics I propose in the paper, human proofs in mathlib capture about 73% of the potential compression available from reusing identical pieces of reasoning, whereas OpenAI's proofs only capture 31% (or 55% against 86% if you look only at proofs that use no automation). Even worse, 40% of OpenAI's proofs are actually larger with their intermediate claims than without them, compared to just 13% in mathlib. The AI seems to be constantly stating intermediate facts that it uses only once or never uses at all. Lastly, while AI proofs look much longer on the surface, most of that length comes from background automation: when you collapse the long, repetitive traces produced by tactics like omega into single steps, the structural gap between human and AI proofs shrinks dramatically.

To make sure my counting tools were working, I checked them against known theorems in proof theory that set hard mathematical limits on how proofs simplify. When the check initially failed on mathlib, it helped me track down and fix several subtle bugs in how my parser was handling definitions and data substitutions. I should also be completely transparent that 100% of the code for this study (the Lean term extractors, the hashing pipeline, and the statistics) was written by Claude Code working under my architectural direction and constraints. The full repository, including all job configurations, regression tests, and raw outputs, is public at [https://github.com/safsom/math-ai-projects] (I am a terrible programmer, so contributions from a good one are very welcome!).

Because Lean's elaboration pipeline has many subtle details that can skew how terms are counted, I would be very grateful for feedback from this community. In particular, I would welcome scrutiny on how compiler-generated auxiliary declarations (_proof_n) are folded back into parent theorems, whether my approach to separating automated tactic steps from human steps makes sense, and whether there are edge cases in how Lean handles definitional equality that might distort my subproof counts. Counterexamples, criticisms, and corrections are all very welcome!
